topic: Déjà vu: prevalence, age, layout familiarity, memory checking, epilepsy link
hook: Déjà vu is your brain checking itself
caption:
That eerie feeling of 'I've lived this before' happens to about two in three people. It's most common in your teens and twenties and fades with age.

One lab finding: déjà vu can appear when a new room shares the layout of a place you've forgotten. Your brain senses the match but can't find the memory. Sources: Brown (2003, Psychological Bulletin) and Cleary et al. (2012).

Follow for one fact your brain won't believe, daily. Tomorrow: why time speeds up as you get older.

When did you last get déjà vu, and where were you?

1/5 Almost everyone gets it (2 in 3)
About two in three people say they've had déjà vu at least once. It's one of the most common odd feelings.
🎨 AI-generated image

2/5 It fades with age (15-25)
It's most frequent in teens and young adults, then shows up less and less as we get older.
📷 Richard Rogerson (CC BY-SA 2.0) via wikimedia

3/5 A layout you forgot
Lab studies show it can appear when a new place has the same layout as one you've seen but can't recall.
📷 AnemoneProjectors (talk) (CC BY-SA 2.0) via wikimedia

4/5 Your brain fact-checking
One leading theory: your brain's memory checker spots a false 'I've seen this' signal and flags it.
📷 John Campbell (CC BY 2.0) via wikimedia

5/5 A seizure warning sign
In temporal lobe epilepsy, déjà vu can come just before a seizure. That helped scientists trace where it starts.
📷 Oliver Taubmann, Martin Berger, Marco Bögel, Yan Xia, Michael Balda, and Andreas (CC BY 4.0) via wikimedia
